tasks.title: Continuous force versus discrete compounding — letter rates
tasks.context: A stock of capital follows the continuous model $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with $P_0>0$ and force $k>0$. A rival discrete model uses the same initial level but annual factor $(1+r)$ with $r>0$, namely $Q(t)=P_0(1+r)^t$. Assume throughout that $1+r\neq e^{k}$ (so the one-year multipliers disagree). Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For every $t>0$, the continuous one-year multiplier equals $1+k$.
The paths $P$ and $Q$ coincide for every $t\ge 0$.
The continuous doubling time is $T=\dfrac{\ln 2}{k}$, independent of $P_0$.
Replacing $e^{kt}$ by $(1+k)^t$ leaves every level $P(t)$ unchanged.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Under continuous force $k$, the one-year multiplier is $e^{k}$.

$$e^{k}\neq 1+k\quad(k\neq 0)$$

So the multiplier is not $1+k$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → False

Two exponential paths with the same $P_0$ agree for all $t$ if and only if their one-year multipliers match.

$$1+r=e^{k}$$

The stem assumes $1+r\neq e^{k}$, so $P$ and $Q$ diverge for $t>0$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

When $r=k>0$, the inequality $e^{k}>1+k$ forces $P(t)>Q(t)$ for $t>0$, so the claimed reverse comparison fails.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Doubling means $P(T)=2P_0$, so $e^{kT}=2$.

$$T=\frac{\ln 2}{k}$$

The initial level $P_0$ cancels, so $T$ depends only on $k$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The substitution $(1+k)^t$ for $e^{kt}$ changes the one-year multiplier from $e^{k}$ to $1+k$. Since $e^{k}\neq 1+k$ for $k>0$, levels move.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Recover the continuous path $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ and the discrete rival $Q(t)=P_0(1+r)^t$. One-year multipliers are $e^{k}$ and $1+r$; they agree for all $t$ precisely when $1+r=e^{k}$. The inequality $e^{k}>1+k$ (for $k>0$) settles the $r=k$ comparison. Doubling solves $e^{kT}=2$, giving $T=\ln 2/k$.

tasks.title: Recovering continuous force from an exact sample table
tasks.context: A positive level $P$ is known to be continuous-exponential, $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with unknown letters $P_0>0$ and $k\in\mathbb{R}$. The table records exact values (not rounded measurements) at four integer times. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For some consecutive pair in the table, $\dfrac{P(t+1)}{P(t)}\neq e^{k}$.
The same table is also generated by the discrete model $P(t)=P_0(1+k)^t$ for every $k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Every consecutive ratio equals $e^{k}$ identically, so the claim fails.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

At $t=0$ one has $P(0)=P_0$, and $P(1)=P_0 e^{k}$.

$$k=\ln\frac{P(1)}{P(0)}$$

That is exactly the recovered force.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Discrete growth with additive rate $k$ would use ratios $1+k$, not $e^{k}$.

$$1+k\neq e^{k}\quad(k\neq 0)$$

So the table is not generated by $P_0(1+k)^t$ for arbitrary $k$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

$$\frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{P(2)}{P(0)}=k$$

The recovered value is $k$, not $2k$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

If $k>0$ then $e^{3k}>e^{2k}$, so $P(3)>P(2)$. The claimed inequality is reversed.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: The table is the exact sampling of $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$. Consecutive ratios are $e^{k}$, so $k=\ln(P(1)/P(0))$ and equally $k=\tfrac12\ln(P(2)/P(0))$. Discrete $(1+k)^t$ matches only in the knife-edge case $1+k=e^{k}$.

tasks.title: Doubling and half-life identities with letter force
tasks.context: Let $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with $P_0>0$. Write $T_{2}=\dfrac{\ln 2}{|k|}$ for the doubling time when $k>0$, and $T_{1/2}=\dfrac{\ln 2}{|k|}$ for the half-life when $k<0$. Both letters denote the same formula in $|k|$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: In both regimes, $T_2$ (or $T_{1/2}$) is independent of $P_0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$T_2=\frac{\ln 2}{k}$$

The factor $\ln 2$ is required; $1/k$ is not the doubling time.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

$$P\!\left(\frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}\right)=P_0 e^{-\lambda\cdot(\ln 2)/\lambda}=P_0 e^{-\ln 2}=\frac12 P_0$$

That is the half-life identity.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

In $e^{kT}=2$ (or $e^{-\lambda T}=\tfrac12$) the factor $P_0$ cancels before taking logs, so the characteristic time depends only on $|k|$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The linearised guess $1/k$ ignores the logarithm.

$$\frac{\ln 2}{k}\neq\frac{1}{k}$$

Exact doubling uses $\ln 2$, not $1$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

$$P(2T_2)=P_0 e^{k\cdot 2(\ln 2)/k}=P_0 e^{2\ln 2}=4P_0$$

Two doubling times multiply the level by four.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Solve $e^{kT}=2$ or $e^{-\lambda T}=\tfrac12$ to obtain $T=\ln 2/|k|$. The initial level cancels. After two doubling times the factor is $2^2=4$.

tasks.title: Two continuous forces $\alpha$ and $\beta$ — parametric comparison
tasks.context: Two positive stocks start equal: $A(0)=B(0)=S_0>0$. Thereafter $A(t)=S_0 e^{\alpha t}$ and $B(t)=S_0 e^{\beta t}$ with letter forces $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\alpha\neq\beta$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $A(t)>B(t)$ for every $t>0$ if and only if $\alpha<\beta$.
The crossing time where $A(t)=B(t)$ for some $t>0$ always exists.
If $\alpha>\beta$, the gap $\ln A(t)-\ln B(t)$ grows linearly in $t$.
Because the starts agree, $A(t)=B(t)$ for every $t$ even though $\alpha\neq\beta$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$\frac{A}{B}=e^{(\alpha-\beta)t}$$

The ratio exceeds $1$ for $t>0$ precisely when $\alpha>\beta$, not $\alpha<\beta$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → False

Since $A(0)=B(0)$ and $\alpha\neq\beta$, the ratio $e^{(\alpha-\beta)t}$ equals $1$ only at $t=0$. There is no later crossing.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

$$\frac{A}{B}=e^{(\alpha-\beta)t}$$

The exponent uses the difference of forces, not the sum.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

$$\ln A(t)-\ln B(t)=(\alpha-\beta)t$$

When $\alpha>\beta$ this linear function of $t$ is strictly increasing.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Equal starts cancel in the ratio, leaving $e^{(\alpha-\beta)t}$, which is not identically $1$ when $\alpha\neq\beta$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: With equal starts, $A/B=e^{(\alpha-\beta)t}$. Sign of $\alpha-\beta$ decides which path leads for all $t>0$; unequal forces never cross again. Log-gap is exactly $(\alpha-\beta)t$.

tasks.title: Rebuild $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ from a doubling time
tasks.context: A continuous-exponential level is known to double every $T>0$ time units: $P(t+T)=2P(t)$ for every $t\ge 0$. It is also known that $P(0)=P_0>0$. No numeric census is supplied — only the letters $P_0$ and $T$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The rebuilt model is linear in $t$: $P(t)=P_0\bigl(1+\dfrac{t\ln 2}{T}\bigr)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Doubling on every window of length $T$ means $e^{kT}=2$.

$$k=\frac{\ln 2}{T}$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$$P(t)=P_0\,2^{t/T}$$

The exponents $t/T$ and $T/t$ are not interchangeable.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

The identity $e^{kT}=2$ yields $k=\ln 2/T$, not $1/T$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

$$P(nT)=2^n P_0$$

Doubling stacks multiplicatively as powers of two, not as $n\cdot 2\,P_0$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The linear expression is the first-order Taylor guess for $e^{(\ln 2)t/T}$, not the exponential solution of the doubling condition.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: From $e^{kT}=2$ recover $k=\ln 2/T$, hence $P(t)=P_0 e^{(\ln 2)t/T}=P_0\,2^{t/T}$. Integer multiples of $T$ produce exact powers of two.

tasks.title: Nested exponential–log compositions with letters
tasks.context: Fix letters $a>0$ and $k\in\mathbb{R}$. Consider the nested expressions $e^{k\ln a}$, $a^{k}$, $\ln(e^{kt})$, and $e^{\ln(P_0)+kt}$ with $P_0>0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For every $a>0$ and every real $k$, $e^{k\ln a}=a^{k}$.
If $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$, then $\ln P(t)=\ln P_0+kt$ for every $t$.
The map $t\mapsto e^{k\ln(1+r)}$ with fixed $r>-1$ equals $(1+r)^{kt}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$e^{k\ln a}=\bigl(e^{\ln a}\bigr)^{k}=a^{k}$$

The identity holds for all $a>0$ and all real $k$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$\ln P(t)=\ln P_0+kt$$

Natural log turns the continuous force into a linear trend.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$e^{\ln P_0+kt}=P_0 e^{kt}$$

Exponent sum becomes a product with $P_0$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Because $\ln$ and $\exp$ are inverses on $\mathbb{R}$,

$$\ln(e^{kt})=kt$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

$$e^{k\ln(1+r)}=(1+r)^{k}$$

There is no extra factor of $t$ in the exponent of the base-$(1+r)$ form.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Use $e^{k\ln a}=a^{k}$ and $\ln\circ\exp=\mathrm{id}$. Continuous growth $P_0 e^{kt}$ is exactly $e^{\ln P_0+kt}$; never rewrite that as a sum.

tasks.title: Semi-log slope reads the letter force $k$
tasks.context: A level follows $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with $P_0>0$. The figure shows an illustrative semi-log plot of $\ln P$ against $t$ for one positive pair $(P_0,k)$. In the letters, the same geometry always holds. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: On the $(t,\ln P)$-plane the graph is a straight line of slope $P_0 k$.
On the $(t,\ln P)$-plane the graph is a straight line of slope $P_0$.
The intercept of that line at $t=0$ equals $\ln P_0$.
Chord slopes equal $k$ only for the special window $[0,1]$.
If $k>0$, the ordinary $(t,P)$-plot is itself a straight line.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$\ln P=\ln P_0+kt$$

The slope is $k$, not $P_0 k$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → False

The slope is the force $k$, not the initial level $P_0$. The letter $P_0$ appears only in the intercept $\ln P_0$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Substitute $t=0$ into $\ln P(t)=\ln P_0+kt$ to read the intercept $\ln P_0$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Because $\ln P$ is exactly linear, every chord equals $k$, not merely the unit window.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

On the raw $(t,P)$-plane one sees $P_0 e^{kt}$, which is curved (convex) for $k\neq 0$, not a straight line.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Take logs once: $\ln P=\ln P_0+kt$. Semi-log slope and every chord equal $k$; intercept is $\ln P_0$. The raw level plot remains exponential.

tasks.title: Tangled quantifiers on continuous exponential paths
tasks.context: Let $\mathcal{E}$ be the family of all functions of the form $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with letters $P_0>0$ and $k\in\mathbb{R}$. Statements below mix universal and existential claims about members of $\mathcal{E}$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: A path $P\in\mathcal{E}$ is strictly increasing on $\mathbb{R}$ if and only if $k\ge 0$.
For every $P\in\mathcal{E}$ with $k\neq 0$, the equation $P(t)=2P_0$ has exactly one real root.
There exists $P\in\mathcal{E}$ such that $P(t)=P_0+kt$ for every $t$.
If $P\in\mathcal{E}$ satisfies $P(t+s)=P(t)P(s)/P_0$ for all real $t,s$, then the functional equation holds automatically for every member of $\mathcal{E}$.
For every $k\in\mathbb{R}$ there is a choice of $P_0>0$ making $P(t)$ identically $1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$P'(t)=k P(t)$$

Strict increase needs $k>0$; the weak inequality $k\ge 0$ wrongly includes the constant case $k=0$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

$$e^{kt}=2\implies t=\frac{\ln 2}{k}$$

For $k\neq 0$ there is exactly one real solution (positive if $k>0$, negative if $k<0$).

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

An exponential $P_0 e^{kt}$ equals the affine path $P_0+kt$ for all $t$ only in degenerate limits that fail for a fixed pair $(P_0,k)$ across every $t$. No such member exists.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Compute for any $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$:

$$\frac{P(t)P(s)}{P_0}=P_0 e^{k(t+s)}=P(t+s)$$

So Cauchy-type scaling holds for the whole family.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Identically $1$ forces $P_0=1$ and $k=0$ simultaneously. For a prescribed nonzero $k$ no choice of $P_0$ works. The universal claim over every $k$ is false.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Sign of $k$ governs monotonicity. Hitting $2P_0$ is a single log solve when $k\neq 0$. Exponentials are not affine. The multiplicative Cauchy identity holds for every $P_0 e^{kt}$.

tasks.title: Piecewise continuous force — switch at letter $T$
tasks.context: A fund follows the piecewise continuous-exponential rule $$P(t)=\begin{cases}P_0 e^{k_1 t},&0\le t\le T,\\[4pt]P_0 e^{k_1 T}e^{k_2(t-T)},&t>T,\end{cases}$$ with letters $P_0>0$, $T>0$, and forces $k_1,k_2\in\mathbb{R}$ (not necessarily equal). Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $P$ jumps discontinuously at the switch time $t=T$.
If $k_1\neq k_2$, then $P$ fails to be continuous at $t=T$.
The average force on $[0,T]$ recovered from $\dfrac{1}{T}\ln\dfrac{P(T)}{P_0}$ equals $k_2$.
One may replace the whole path by the single force $k_1$ for all $t\ge 0$ without changing any value, even when $k_2\neq k_1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$P(T-)=P(T+)=P_0 e^{k_1 T}$$

The pieced definition is continuous at $T$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → False

Continuity at $T$ uses only the matching value $P_0 e^{k_1 T}$; it does not require $k_1=k_2$. A kink in the derivative can occur while the level stays continuous.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

For $t>T$, take logs of the second piece:

$$\ln P(t)=\ln P_0+k_1 T+k_2(t-T)$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

$$\frac{1}{T}\ln\frac{P(T)}{P_0}=k_1$$

The early window sees force $k_1$, not $k_2$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

After $T$, the true force is $k_2$. Whenever $k_2\neq k_1$ the constant-$k_1$ extrapolation disagrees for $t>T$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Match values at $T$ to keep continuity; log-linearise each piece separately. Early average force is $k_1$. A single global force $k_1$ cannot replace a genuine switch.

tasks.title: GDP per capita — force $g-p$ trap with letter rates
tasks.context: Aggregate real output and population follow $Y(t)=Y_0 e^{gt}$ and $N(t)=N_0 e^{pt}$ with letters $Y_0,N_0>0$ and forces $g,p\in\mathbb{R}$. Per capita output is the ratio $y(t)=Y(t)/N(t)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The continuous force on $y$ is exactly $g-p$.
The continuous force on $y$ is exactly $g+p$.
If $g>0$ and $p>0$, then necessarily $y$ is strictly increasing.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$\ln y=\ln Y-\ln N=\ln Y_0-\ln N_0+(g-p)t$$

Differentiating (or reading the coefficient of $t$) shows the force is $g-p$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Adding forces would describe a product $YN$, not the ratio $Y/N$. The sum trap $g+p$ is not the per-capita force.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

$$y(t)=y_0 e^{(g-p)t}$$

Per capita carries the difference force, not the sum.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Differentiate $\ln y=\mathrm{const}+(g-p)t$ to obtain $g-p$ at every $t$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Growth of $y$ requires $g-p>0$, not merely $g>0$ and $p>0$. If population force exceeds output force, per capita falls.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Logs turn the ratio into a difference of forces: $\ln y=\ln y_0+(g-p)t$. Never add $g$ and $p$ for per capita. Sign of $g-p$ alone governs whether $y$ rises.

tasks.title: Competing populations with letter rates $k_A,k_B$
tasks.context: Two populations obey $A(t)=A_0 e^{k_A t}$ and $B(t)=B_0 e^{k_B t}$ with $A_0,B_0>0$ and real forces $k_A,k_B$. The figure is an illustration for one positive-rate scenario; claims stay in letters. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The time at which $A(t)=B(t)$ (when it exists and is unique) solves $t=\dfrac{\ln(B_0/A_0)}{k_A-k_B}$ provided $k_A\neq k_B$ and the right-hand side is positive.
Equal initial levels $A_0=B_0$ force $A(t)=B(t)$ for every $t$, regardless of $k_A,k_B$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$\frac{A}{B}=\frac{A_0}{B_0}e^{(k_A-k_B)t}\to\infty$$

The ratio diverges, rather than tending to $0$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Set $A_0 e^{k_A t}=B_0 e^{k_B t}$ and take logs:

$$t=\frac{\ln(B_0/A_0)}{k_A-k_B}$$

Whenever this $t$ is positive it is the unique crossing.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

A larger start can still be overtaken when the rival force is larger. The claim that $A$ stays ahead forever is false in general.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

$$\frac{d}{dt}\ln\frac{A}{B}=k_A-k_B$$

The log-ratio grows at the force gap, not the sum.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Equal starts give $A/B=e^{(k_A-k_B)t}$, which stays $1$ for all $t$ only if $k_A=k_B$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Compare via the ratio $A/B=(A_0/B_0)e^{(k_A-k_B)t}$. Crossings are a single log solve; long-run leadership follows the larger force.

tasks.title: Diagnosing discrete versus continuous from a twin table
tasks.context: Two positive processes are tabulated exactly. $U$ is proposed as discrete annual compounding with letter factor $(1+r)$, $r>-1$, $r\neq 0$. $V$ is proposed as continuous force $k\neq 0$. Initial levels $U_0,V_0>0$ are letters. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The successive ratios of $U$ are constant and equal to $1+r$.
If $1+r=e^{k}$ and $U_0=V_0$, then the tabulated values still disagree at $t=2$.
Constant successive ratios are incompatible with any exponential model.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$\frac{U(1)}{U(0)}=1+r,\quad \frac{U(2)}{U(1)}=1+r$$

Discrete compounding has constant ratio $1+r$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$$\frac{V(t+1)}{V(t)}=e^{k}$$

Continuous force yields ratio $e^{k}$, not $1+k$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

When $1+r=e^{k}$ and starts agree, both models produce the same geometric sequence, so the $t=2$ entries match. The claim that they disagree is false.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Constant ratios are the hallmark of pure exponential (discrete or continuous) structure.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The table never equates $r$ with $k$; it only exhibits ratios $1+r$ and $e^{k}$. Those letters may differ.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Read constant ratios off each row: $1+r$ for discrete, $e^{k}$ for continuous. The models coincide on the grid precisely when $1+r=e^{k}$ and starts match — not when $r=k$.

tasks.title: Newton cooling structure with ambient letter $T_a$
tasks.context: A temperature $T(t)$ obeys Newton cooling toward a constant ambient letter $T_a$: $$T(t)=T_a+\bigl(T(0)-T_a\bigr)e^{-kt},$$ with force letter $k>0$ and $T(0)\neq T_a$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The gap $T(t)-T_a$ is a pure exponential with force $+k$.
The path $T(t)$ itself is a pure exponential $Ce^{kt}$ through the origin of temperature.
Solving $T(t)=T_\ast$ for a target between $T(0)$ and $T_a$ yields $t=\dfrac{1}{k}\ln\dfrac{T(0)-T_a}{T_\ast-T_a}$.
If $T(0)>T_a$, then $T(t)$ is increasing for all $t>0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$T(t)-T_a=\bigl(T(0)-T_a\bigr)e^{-kt}\to 0$$

Hence $T(t)\to T_a$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$$T(t)-T_a=(T(0)-T_a)e^{-kt}$$

The gap force is $-k$, not $+k$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Unless $T_a=0$, the level $T(t)$ is an exponential plus a nonzero constant, not a pure through-origin exponential.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Set $T_a+(T(0)-T_a)e^{-kt}=T_\ast$ and rearrange:

$$e^{-kt}=\frac{T_\ast-T_a}{T(0)-T_a}$$

$$t=\frac{1}{k}\ln\frac{T(0)-T_a}{T_\ast-T_a}$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

When $T(0)>T_a$ the object cools toward ambient, so $T$ is decreasing, not increasing.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Rewrite Newton as an exponential gap to $T_a$. Long-run limit is ambient; hitting times are log solves on the gap. The temperature level is affine-plus-exponential, not a pure $Ce^{kt}$.

tasks.title: Matching discrete factor $(1+r)$ to continuous force $k$
tasks.context: A bank offers discrete annual growth with letter factor $(1+r)$, $r>-1$. A continuous rival uses force $k\in\mathbb{R}$. Both start at the same $P_0>0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The two models agree at every integer year if and only if $e^{k}=1+r$.
Setting $k=r$ fails to match the models at integer years whenever $r\neq 0$.
The continuous force that matches the discrete factor is $k=\ln(1+r)$ (for $r>-1$).
For $r>0$, the matching force $\ln(1+r)$ is strictly smaller than $r$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

At integer $n$, discrete gives $P_0(1+r)^n$ while continuous gives $P_0 e^{kn}$. Equality for all $n$ holds iff $e^{k}=1+r$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Unless $r=0$, one has $e^{r}\neq 1+r$, so $k=r$ does not match discrete compounding.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$k=\ln(1+r)$$

That is the unique continuous force matching the discrete factor.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$\ln(1+r)<r\quad(r>0)$$

Strict concavity of $\ln$ yields the inequality.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

$$\ln(1+r)<r\quad(r>0)$$

The inequality goes the other way.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Equate one-year multipliers: $e^{k}=1+r$ forces $k=\ln(1+r)$. The naive $k=r$ overstates continuous force relative to discrete factor when $r>0$.
tasks.tables_markdown:
| spelling | one-year factor | continuous force |
| --- | --- | --- |
| discrete | $1+r$ | — |
| matched continuous | $e^{k}$ | $k=\ln(1+r)$ |
| naive $k=r$ | $e^{r}$ | $r$ |

tasks.title: Rebuild continuous force from two lettered observations
tasks.context: A continuous-exponential path passes through two observations $\bigl(t_1,P(t_1)\bigr)$ and $\bigl(t_2,P(t_2)\bigr)$ with $t_2>t_1$ and positive levels. Letters $P(t_i)$ stand for the observed values. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The recovered force is $k=\dfrac{\ln P(t_2)-\ln P(t_1)}{t_2-t_1}$.
The rebuilt path may be written $P(t)=P(t_1)\,e^{k(t+t_1)}$ with that $k$.
The same two points always determine a unique discrete factor $(1+r)$ that matches them at every real $t$, not merely on an integer grid.
A third off-path observation is still compatible with the same pure continuous-exponential model.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$k=\frac{\ln P(t_2)-\ln P(t_1)}{t_2-t_1}$$

That is the unique continuous force through the two points.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$$P(t)=P(t_1)e^{k(t-t_1)}$$

The correct time shift is $t-t_1$, not $t+t_1$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

A discrete factor $(1+r)^t$ is not even defined the same way for non-integer $t$ without extending via $\exp(t\ln(1+r))$, which then collapses to a continuous force. There is no separate discrete path that matches two points at every real $t$ while remaining a different model.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Three inconsistent points overdetermine and reject a two-parameter exponential.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The difference quotient of raw levels is not the continuous force; force uses logs.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Two positive observations fix $k$ via a log chord and then fix the whole path by anchoring at one point. Raw slopes are not forces; a third off-path point rejects the model.

tasks.title: Rewriting $a^{t}$ as continuous force $\ln a$
tasks.context: Fix a letter base $a>0$, $a\neq 1$, and write $f(t)=a^{t}$. View $f$ as a continuous-exponential path. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$a^{t}=e^{t\ln a}$$

Definition of real exponentiation.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Force is the coefficient of $t$ in the exponent after writing $e^{(\cdot)t}$, namely $\ln a$, not the base $a$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

$$a^{t}=e^{t\ln a}$$

Force is $\ln a$, not the discrete net $a-1$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

$$a^{T}=2\implies T\ln a=\ln 2\implies T=\frac{\ln 2}{\ln a}$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Writing $a=1+(a-1)$ does not convert the continuous force into $a-1$. Force remains $\ln a$, while $a-1$ is a discrete one-year net rate relative to $1$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Pass to $e^{t\ln a}$ to read force $\ln a$. Doubling solves $a^{T}=2$. Do not confuse $\ln a$ with the discrete net $a-1$.

tasks.title: Hybrid — integer doubling table meets continuous force $\ln 2$
tasks.context: The table records exact levels of a continuous-exponential path at integer times. The figure sketches the same path. Treat the pattern as $P(t)=e^{kt}$ with unknown letter $k$ to be recovered (here $P_0=1$). Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The same table is not generated by force $k=2$.
Matching the integer grid fixes $P_0$ and $k$, so the continuous extension beyond integers is unique.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$e^{k}=2\implies k=\ln 2$$

The force is $\ln 2$, not $2$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

$$P(t)=e^{(\ln 2)t}=2^{t}$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

With $k=\ln 2$, doubling time is $\ln 2/k=1$, matching the table's step.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Force $k=2$ would give ratios $e^{2}$, not $2$, so it does not generate the table.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

A continuous exponential is completely determined by $P_0$ and $k$. The integer samples pin both letters, so non-integer values are determined.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Ratio $2$ forces $k=\ln 2$ and $P(t)=2^{t}$. Doubling time is $1$. The continuous extension beyond integers is unique.

tasks.title: ‘For every’ and ‘precisely when’ in exponential claims
tasks.context: Throughout, $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with $P_0>0$. Quantifiers range over real times and over letter parameters as written. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For every $k\in\mathbb{R}$, $P$ is unbounded above on $[0,\infty)$.
$P$ is unbounded above on $[0,\infty)$ precisely when $k>0$.
For every $P_0>0$ and every $k$, the identity $P(0)=2P_0$ holds.
For every $t>0$, the map $k\mapsto P(t)$ is decreasing.
The equality $P(t)=P_0$ for every $t$ holds precisely when $k=0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

If $k\le 0$ then $P$ is bounded on $[0,\infty)$ (constant or decaying). The universal claim over every $k$ fails.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

For $k>0$, $P(t)\to\infty$. For $k\le 0$ it does not. That is precisely the dichotomy.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

$$P(0)=P_0$$

The initial value is $P_0$, not $2P_0$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial k}P(t)=t P_0 e^{kt}>0\quad(t>0)$$

So $k\mapsto P(t)$ is increasing in $k$, not decreasing.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

$P(t)=P_0$ for all $t$ iff $e^{kt}=1$ for all $t$ iff $k=0$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Read quantifiers carefully: unboundedness needs $k>0$; constancy needs $k=0$. Partial derivatives in $k$ show larger force raises every positive-time level.

tasks.title: Piecewise growth then decay — letters $k_+,k_-$
tasks.context: A biomarker follows force $k_+>0$ on $[0,T]$ and force $-k_-$ with $k_->0$ after $T$: $$P(t)=\begin{cases}P_0 e^{k_+ t},&0\le t\le T,\P_0 e^{k_+ T}e^{-k_-(t-T)},&t>T.\end{cases}$$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The peak value on $[0,\infty)$ equals $P(T)=P_0 e^{k_+ T}$.
For $t>T$, the half-life relative to the peak is $\dfrac{\ln 2}{k_+}$.
$\ln P$ rises with slope $k_+$ before $T$ and falls with slope $-k_-$ afterward.
If $k_+=k_-$, the path is symmetric about $t=T$ in calendar time for all horizons.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Before $T$ the path rises; after $T$ it falls. Continuity at $T$ makes $P(T)$ the global peak.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

After $T$ the decay force is $k_-$, so the half-life is $\ln 2/k_-$, not $\ln 2/k_+$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

$$P(t)=P(T)e^{-k_-(t-T)}\to 0$$

not $P_0$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Log-linear slopes are exactly the instantaneous forces on each piece.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Equal magnitudes make the rise and fall rates match, but symmetry about $t=T$ for all horizons would also require mirroring the time domain; decay continues forever while growth only occupied $[0,T]$, so global calendar symmetry fails.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Peak at the switch, then exponential decay to $0$ with half-life $\ln 2/k_-$. Semi-log slopes flip from $+k_+$ to $-k_-$.

tasks.title: Unit trap — letter $M$ millions versus raw counts
tasks.context: A city population is reported as $M(t)$ million residents with $M(t)=M_0 e^{kt}$, letters $M_0>0$ and $k\in\mathbb{R}$. The raw headcount is $H(t)=10^6\,M(t)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $H$ obeys the same continuous force $k$ as $M$.
Doubling time for $H$ is one million times the doubling time for $M$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$H(t)=10^6 M_0 e^{kt}$$

A positive constant factor does not change continuous force, so $H$ still has force $k$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Doubling solves $e^{kT}=2$ for both series; the $10^6$ cancels. Doubling times coincide.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

$$\ln H=\ln M+\ln(10^6)$$

The raw headcount adds $\ln(10^6)$, rather than subtracting it.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Differentiating the previous display shows both semi-log slopes equal $k$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

If $M_0=3$ (millions), then $H(0)=3\cdot 10^6$, not $3$. That is the unit trap.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Changing units by a positive constant rescales the level but preserves force, doubling time, and semi-log slope. Never drop the $10^6$ when reading headcount.

tasks.title: Reading a continuous growth graph in letters
tasks.context: The figure illustrates a path of the form $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with $P_0>0$, $k>0$. Interpret all claims in those letters (the sketch uses one admissible pair). Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The elasticity $\dfrac{t P'(t)}{P(t)}$ equals $k$ (with no factor of $t$).
For every $c>1$ there is a unique $T>0$ with $P(T)=c P_0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$P''(t)=k^{2} P_0 e^{kt}>0$$

for $k\neq 0$, so with $k>0$ the path is strictly convex.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$$\frac{t P'(t)}{P(t)}=kt$$

An extra factor of $t$ remains.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

$$P''(t)=k^{2} P(t)>0$$

for $k\neq 0$ and finite $t$, so $P''$ has no root.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$\frac{P'(t)}{P(t)}=k$$

that constant is the continuous force.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

$$T=\frac{\ln c}{k}>0$$

unique because $P$ is strictly increasing.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Differentiate $P_0 e^{kt}$ to read constant relative rate $k$, positive second derivative, and unique hitting times $T=\ln c/k$ for each multiple $c>1$.

tasks.title: Equal log-increments diagnose constant force $k$
tasks.context: An analyst tabulates log-increments of a positive series $P$ over successive unit windows and finds they all equal the same letter $k$. Assume $P$ is continuous and strictly positive. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: On each integer window the continuous average force equals $k$.
The table alone proves $P$ cannot be discrete-geometric with factor $e^{k}$.
If $P$ is known a priori to be continuous-exponential, then its force equals $2k$.
Equal unit-window log-increments force $P$ to be linear in $t$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

By definition the average force on $[n,n+1]$ is the log-increment, here equal to $k$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Discrete geometry with ratio $e^{k}$ produces exactly these log-increments on the integer grid. The table does not rule that model out.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Constant unit log-increments of size $k$ identify the force as $k$, not $2k$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Chaining $n$ unit increments of size $k$ multiplies by $e^{kn}$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Equal log-increments produce exponential (or geometric) behaviour, not affine linearity.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Constant log-increments mean constant average force on each window. On the integer grid this matches both $e^{kt}$ and geometric $(e^{k})^{n}$. It does not yield a line.

tasks.title: Radioactive-style decay with letter rate $\lambda$
tasks.context: A mass follows $m(t)=m_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ with letters $m_0>0$ and $\lambda>0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Time to reach fraction $f\in(0,1)$ of $m_0$ is $t=\dfrac{\ln f}{\lambda}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}}=\frac12\implies T_{1/2}=\frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$m(n T_{1/2})=m_0 e^{-\ln 2\cdot n}=2^{-n}m_0$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$m(t)=m_0 e^{-\lambda t}$$

Reading the exponent shows force $k=-\lambda$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$\frac{m'}{m}=-\lambda$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

$$t=\frac{-\ln f}{\lambda}$$

Because $\ln f<0$, the correct expression carries a minus sign (equivalently $\ln(1/f)/\lambda$).

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Decay force is $-\lambda$. Half-life $\ln 2/\lambda$ stacks as powers of $\tfrac12$. General fraction $f$ solves by the same log.

tasks.title: Per capita with growth letters $\alpha$ and population $\beta$
tasks.context: Rename the earlier macro forces: output grows at letter $\alpha$ and population at letter $\beta$, so $Y=Y_0 e^{\alpha t}$, $N=N_0 e^{\beta t}$, and $y=Y/N$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Maximising $\alpha$ alone always maximises the force on $y$, holding nothing else fixed in a comparative-static sense is automatic even if $\beta$ rises one-for-one with $\alpha$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Same log-ratio argument as with $(g,p)$: force on $y$ is $\alpha-\beta$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

When $\alpha=\beta$ the force on $y$ is $0$, not $\alpha$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

$$y(t)=y(0)e^{0\cdot t}=y(0)$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

If $\beta$ rises one-for-one with $\alpha$, the difference $\alpha-\beta$ is unchanged. Raising $\alpha$ alone need not raise per-capita force when $\beta$ co-moves.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Integrate force $\alpha-\beta$ from the initial level $y(0)$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Per-capita force is the difference $\alpha-\beta$. Equal forces freeze $y$. Watch co-movement of population force when comparing policies.

tasks.title: Rebuild decay from a lettered half-life
tasks.context: A decaying continuous-exponential mass has half-life letter $H>0$ and initial mass $m_0>0$. Rebuild $m(t)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The rebuilt model has positive continuous force.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$e^{kH}=\frac12\implies k=-\frac{\ln 2}{H}$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$$m(t)=m_0\,2^{-t/H}=m_0 e^{-(\ln 2)t/H}$$

Decay needs the negative exponent; the claimed positive exponent describes growth.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

The positive exponent $2^{t/H}$ would describe growth, contradicting half-life decay.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

$$m(H/2)=m_0\,2^{-1/2}=m_0/\sqrt{2}$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Force $k=-(\ln 2)/H$ is negative.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Half-life $H$ means $e^{kH}=\tfrac12$, so $k=-(\ln 2)/H$ and $m(t)=m_0 2^{-t/H}$.

tasks.title: Nested form $e^{k\ln(P/Q)}$ as a relative power
tasks.context: Let $P,Q>0$ be positive letter levels and $k\in\mathbb{R}$. Study the nested scalar $e^{k\ln(P/Q)}$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $k=0$, the nested expression equals $1$ for every positive $P,Q$.
The identity $e^{k\ln(P/Q)}=k\ln(P/Q)$ fails for some choices of $k\neq 0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$e^{k\ln(P/Q)}=(P/Q)^{k}$$

The base is $P/Q$, not its reciprocal.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

$$k\ln(P/Q)=k\ln P-k\ln Q$$

Exponentiating preserves the split.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$e^{0}=1$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$e^{k\ln 1}=e^{0}=1$$

Equal positive levels force the log argument to $1$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Exponential and identity maps agree only at special points. For example $k=1$, $P/Q=e$ gives $e\neq 1$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Collapse $e^{k\ln(P/Q)}$ to $(P/Q)^{k}$. Special cases: $k=0$ gives $1$; $P=Q$ gives $1$.

tasks.title: Hybrid — equal starts, letter force gap $\delta$
tasks.context: Two funds start equal, $A_0=B_0=S_0>0$, with forces $k$ and $k+\delta$ where the gap letter satisfies $\delta\neq 0$. Thus $A(t)=S_0 e^{kt}$ and $B(t)=S_0 e^{(k+\delta)t}$. The figure illustrates $\delta>0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The funds do not cross again at any $t>0$.
If $\delta>0$, then $B$ eventually dominates $A$ by an arbitrarily large factor.
The force gap $\delta$ equals $\dfrac{B(t)-A(t)}{t}$ for every $t>0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$B/A=e^{\delta t}$$

There is no additive $+1$ on the right-hand side.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Equal starts and $\delta\neq 0$ prevent any later crossing.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$e^{\delta t}\to\infty$ when $\delta>0$, so the factor $B/A$ is arbitrarily large.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$\ln B-\ln A=\delta t$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The raw gap $B-A$ is not linear in $t$ with slope $\delta$; log-gap is.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Equal starts cancel, leaving pure gap factor $e^{\delta t}$. Leadership is decided by the sign of $\delta$; raw level gaps are not the force gap.

tasks.title: Compound claims linking discrete and continuous letters
tasks.context: A portfolio may be viewed either as $P_0(1+r)^{t}$ with $r>-1$ or as $P_0 e^{kt}$ with $k=\ln(1+r)$. Claims combine both spellings. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: With $k=\ln(1+r)$, the two spellings define the same function only at integer $t$.
With $k=\ln(1+r)$, doubling time is not $\dfrac{\ln 2}{r}$ whenever $r\neq\ln(1+r)$.
For $r>0$, matching continuous force is strictly smaller than the discrete net rate $r$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$P_0(1+r)^{t}=P_0 e^{t\ln(1+r)}$$

The identity holds for every real $t$, not merely integers.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Doubling uses denominator $k=\ln(1+r)$. Since $\ln(1+r)\neq r$ for $r\neq 0$, the time is not $\ln 2/r$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$T=\frac{\ln 2}{k}=\frac{\ln 2}{\ln(1+r)}$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Since $\ln(1+r)<r$ for $r>0$, the reciprocal reverses the inequality, yielding $\ln 2/\ln(1+r)>\ln 2/r$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

$$\ln(1+r)<r\quad(r>0)$$

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Identify $k=\ln(1+r)$ to unify spellings. Doubling is $\ln 2/\ln(1+r)$, which exceeds the naive $\ln 2/r$ because $\ln(1+r)<r$.

tasks.title: Policy switch raising force after letter $T$
tasks.context: Capital grows at force $k_1$ until a reform date $T>0$, then at a higher force $k_2>k_1$: the standard piecewise continuous-exponential definition applies with letters $P_0>0$, $k_1$, $k_2$, $T$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Ignoring the reform and using force $k_1$ forever understates $P(t)$ for every $t>T$.
For every $t>T$, the true path strictly exceeds the constant-$k_1$ extrapolation from time $0$.
At $t=T$, both the true path and the no-reform path agree.
The true path after $T$ equals $P_0 e^{k_2 t}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

After $T$ the true force $k_2>k_1$ is larger, so the no-reform path lies strictly below the true path.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$P_0 e^{k_1 T}e^{k_2(t-T)}>P_0 e^{k_1 t}\iff k_2(t-T)>k_1(t-T)$$

which holds because $k_2>k_1$ and $t>T$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Both paths equal $P_0 e^{k_1 T}$ at the switch.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

That formula would apply only if force $k_2$ had been used from time $0$. The early window still used $k_1$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

That is exactly the second piece of the definition.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Match at $T$, then apply $k_2$. Constant-$k_1$ extrapolation understates post-reform levels when $k_2>k_1$. Do not pretend $k_2$ applied from time zero.

tasks.title: Applied Newton — ambient $T_a$ and force $k$ as letters
tasks.context: Coffee cools in a room at ambient letter $T_a$ according to $T(t)=T_a+(T_0-T_a)e^{-kt}$ with $T_0>T_a$ and $k>0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The time to the midpoint $\dfrac{T_0+T_a}{2}$ equals $\dfrac{\ln 2}{k}$.
Raising $k$ shortens every hitting time to a fixed interior target between $T_a$ and $T_0$.
Raising $T_a$ while holding $T_0,k$ fixed leaves all hitting times to levels above the old $T_a$ unchanged.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The gap factor $e^{-kt}\in(0,1)$ for $t>0$ keeps $T(t)$ strictly between $T_a$ and $T_0$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The gap stays positive, so $T(t)$ approaches $T_a$ from above and never crosses it.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Midpoint means the gap has halved:

$$e^{-kt}=\frac12\implies t=\frac{\ln 2}{k}$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Hitting-time formulas have $1/k$ in front; larger $k$ shortens times.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Changing ambient reshapes every gap $T_\ast-T_a$, so hitting times move.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Cooling stays trapped between $T_0$ and $T_a$. Half-gap time is $\ln 2/k$. Force scales all clocks; ambient shifts targets.

tasks.title: Graph comparison — force $k$ versus factor $1+r$
tasks.context: The figure sketches $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ against $Q(t)=P_0(1+r)^{t}$ for one positive pair with $e^{k}\neq 1+r$. Interpret claims in letters $P_0>0$, $k$, $r>-1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Both paths share the same initial value $P_0$.
The discrete path lies strictly below the continuous path whenever $r=k>0$.
With fixed unequal multipliers, the two paths cannot touch at three distinct positive times.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$\frac{P}{Q}=e^{(k-\ln(1+r))t}$$

When $k>\ln(1+r)$ and $t>0$ the ratio exceeds $1$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Both formulas give $P_0$ at $t=0$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

For $r=k>0$ one has $e^{k}>1+k$, so continuous lies above discrete for $t>0$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Log-gap is linear in $t$, so agreement occurs at most at $t=0$ unless multipliers match (in which case they agree everywhere).

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

$$\ln P-\ln Q=\bigl(k-\ln(1+r)\bigr)t$$

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Compare via $P/Q=\exp\bigl((k-\ln(1+r))t\bigr)$. Shared start; at most one agreement time unless forces match. For $r=k>0$ continuous wins.

tasks.title: Recover discrete letter $r$ from a geometric table
tasks.context: A balance follows exact discrete compounding $Q(t)=Q_0(1+r)^{t}$ on the integer grid, with letters $Q_0>0$ and $r>-1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The one-year growth rate in percent is $100(1+r)$ (as a letter expression).
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$1+r=\frac{Q(1)}{Q(0)}\implies r=\frac{Q(1)}{Q(0)}-1$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$k=\ln(1+r)=\ln\frac{Q(1)}{Q(0)}$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Only in the knife-edge $r=0$ does $k=r$; generally $k=\ln(1+r)\neq r$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

$$\frac{Q(3)}{Q(1)}=(1+r)^{2}$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The net one-year rate is $r$, so the percent expression is $100r$, not $100(1+r)$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Read $1+r$ from the first ratio; convert to continuous force by a logarithm. Multi-year ratios are powers of $1+r$.

tasks.title: Ordering continuous forces without numeric drills
tasks.context: Three continuous-exponential paths share the same $P_0>0$ but use forces $k_1<k_2<k_3$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For every $t>0$, $P_0 e^{k_1 t}<P_0 e^{k_2 t}<P_0 e^{k_3 t}$.
Semi-log slopes increase strictly in the index $i$.
If each force is replaced by its negative, then for every $t>0$ one has $P_0 e^{-k_1 t}>P_0 e^{-k_2 t}>P_0 e^{-k_3 t}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The map $k\mapsto e^{kt}$ is increasing for each fixed $t>0$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Larger force shortens doubling time, so $T_1>T_2>T_3$, not the claimed increasing order.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

$$T_i=\frac{\ln 2}{k_i}$$

hence $k_1<k_2<k_3$ implies $T_1>T_2>T_3$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Semi-log slope equals the force, so slopes inherit $k_1<k_2<k_3$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Negating reverses the order of forces, and therefore reverses the order of levels at each $t>0$.

$$e^{-k_1 t}>e^{-k_2 t}>e^{-k_3 t}$$

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Larger force raises every positive-time level and steepens semi-log slope, but shortens doubling time. Negating all forces reverses which index leads.

tasks.title: Parametric family $P_\lambda(t)=P_0 e^{\lambda t}$
tasks.context: Index a family of paths by a force letter $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$: $P_\lambda(t)=P_0 e^{\lambda t}$ with fixed $P_0>0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For each fixed $t>0$, $\lambda\mapsto P_\lambda(t)$ is strictly increasing.
$P_\lambda$ coincides with $P_\mu$ as functions on $\mathbb{R}$ if and only if $\lambda=\mu$.
$P_\lambda(t)=P_{-\lambda}(-t)$ holds for every real $\lambda$ and every real $t$.
The map $\lambda\mapsto T_2(\lambda)=\dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$ (for $\lambda>0$) is strictly decreasing.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$\partial_\lambda P_\lambda(t)=t P_0 e^{\lambda t}>0\quad(t>0)$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

If $\lambda\neq\mu$ then already at $t=1$ the values $P_0 e^{\lambda}$ and $P_0 e^{\mu}$ differ.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$P_0 e^{\lambda t}=P_0 e^{(-\lambda)(-t)}$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$e^{2}=e^{(-1)\cdot(-2)}$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

As $\lambda$ rises, $\ln 2/\lambda$ falls.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Force indexes the family injectively. Time reversal pairs $\lambda$ with $-\lambda$. Doubling time decreases in $\lambda$.

tasks.title: Rebuild from one point and a letter force
tasks.context: A continuous-exponential path has known force $k$ and passes through a single observation $(t_\ast,P_\ast)$ with $P_\ast>0$. Rebuild $P(t)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The implied initial level is $P_0=P_\ast e^{-k t_\ast}$.
Doubling time (if $k>0$) remains $\dfrac{\ln 2}{k}$, independent of the observation.
The observation alone, without $k$, does not determine the entire path.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$P(t)=P_\ast e^{k(t-t_\ast)}$$

The anchor shift is $t-t_\ast$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → False

Omitting the time shift would force the observation to lie at $t=0$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

$$P_0=P(0)=P_\ast e^{-k t_\ast}$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Doubling depends only on force, not on where the path was observed.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

One point leaves a one-parameter family; the force letter is required to pin $k$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Anchor at the observation: $P(t)=P_\ast e^{k(t-t_\ast)}$. Back out $P_0$ if needed. Characteristic times still depend only on $k$.

tasks.title: Nested $\ln$ of a continuous path
tasks.context: Let $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with $P_0>0$. Compare single and double logarithms of the path. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: There exist $P_0>e$ and $k>0$ such that $\ln\ln P(t)$ is defined for all large $t$ yet $\ln\ln P(t)\neq kt$ for some such $t$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$\ln P(t)=\ln P_0+kt$$

Logs turn products into sums, not products of the log pieces.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

$$\ln(e^{kt})=kt$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

$$\ln\ln P(t)=\ln(\ln P_0+kt)$$

This equals $kt$ only in nongeneric cases, not for every $P_0>e$ and every $t\ge 0$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Take $P_0=e^{2}$ and $k=1$. Then $\ln\ln P(t)=\ln(2+t)$, which differs from $t$ at $t=1$ since $\ln 3\neq 1$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

$$e^{\ln P+kt}=P e^{kt}=P_0 e^{2kt}$$

$$P^{2}=P_0^{2} e^{2kt}$$

Equality for every $t$ forces $P_0=1$, contradicting universality over every $P_0>0$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Single logs linearise continuous exponentials. Double logs produce $\ln(\ln P_0+kt)$, not $kt$. Algebraic slips with $e^{\ln P+kt}$ introduce extra factors.

tasks.title: Hybrid semi-log table — slope letter $k$
tasks.context: The table lists exact log-levels of $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$. The figure sketches the semi-log geometry for one positive pair. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The chord from $t=0$ to $t=4$ has slope $4k$.
The chord from $t=2$ to $t=4$ has slope $k$.
The table is inconsistent with force $2k$ in place of $k$.
Exponentiating the middle entry recovers $P(2)=P_0 e^{2k}$.
If $k<0$, the semi-log plot slopes upward.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$\frac{4k}{4}=k$$

The chord slope equals $k$, not $4k$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

$$\frac{(\ln P_0+4k)-(\ln P_0+2k)}{2}=k$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Force $2k$ would produce increments $4k$ and $8k$ over those windows, contradicting the table.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$P(2)=e^{\ln P_0+2k}=P_0 e^{2k}$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Negative $k$ yields a downward semi-log slope.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Every chord on $\ln P=\ln P_0+kt$ returns slope $k$. Exponentiate to recover levels. Sign of $k$ is the sign of the semi-log slope.

tasks.title: Precisely-when criteria for exponential structure
tasks.context: Let $P:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ be differentiable. Consider criteria that characterise continuous-exponential form $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $P'/P$ constant on $(0,\infty)$ if and only if $P$ is continuous-exponential.
$\ln P$ affine on $(0,\infty)$ if and only if $P$ is continuous-exponential.
$P''>0$ everywhere does not by itself characterise continuous-exponential structure.
Constant successive ratios on every pair of times distance $1$ apart are necessary for continuous-exponential structure.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The ODE $P'=kP$ with $P>0$ integrates to $P(t)=Ce^{kt}$. Conversely every continuous exponential has constant relative rate.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Affinity of $\ln P$ is the integrated form of the same criterion.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Strict convexity holds for many non-exponential positives (e.g. $t^{2}+1$ on $(0,\infty)$).

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Continuous exponentials have $P(t+1)/P(t)=e^{k}$ constantly — necessity holds.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Integrate from the anchor $t=1$ to obtain that shifted formula.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Constant relative rate, or affine log, characterises continuous exponentials. Convexity is weaker. Unit-lag ratios are constant for this class.

tasks.title: Average force across a piecewise exponential
tasks.context: Take the piecewise path with forces $k_1$ on $[0,T]$ and $k_2$ on $(T,t_\bullet]$ for a horizon $t_\bullet>T$, starting at $P_0>0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The average force on $[0,t_\bullet]$ equals $k_1 T+k_2(t_\bullet-T)$ without dividing by $t_\bullet$.
That average depends on $T$ and $t_\bullet$ in general, not merely on $(k_1+k_2)/2$.
Average force equals the arithmetic mean of the endpoint relative rates $\tfrac12\bigl(P'(0)/P(0)+P'(t_\bullet)/P(t_\bullet)\bigr)$ even when $k_1\neq k_2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$\frac{k_1 T+k_2(t_\bullet-T)}{t_\bullet}$$

Average force divides the accumulated log growth by elapsed time.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Weights are the time spent in each regime; they need not be equal half-and-half, so the average is not automatically $(k_1+k_2)/2$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Chain the two exponential pieces to obtain that product of factors.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Equal forces make the weighted average equal to the common force.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Endpoint relative rates are $k_1$ and $k_2$, whose arithmetic mean ignores time weights and generally differs from the duration-weighted average.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Average force is duration-weighted: $(k_1 T+k_2(t_\bullet-T))/t_\bullet$. It equals the plain mean of endpoint forces only in symmetric special cases.

tasks.title: Applied — when per capita force vanishes
tasks.context: Output and population forces are letters $g$ and $p$. Per capita is $y=Y/N$ with the usual continuous-exponential aggregates. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $y$ is constant for every choice of $g,p$.
If $g=p$, then $Y$ and $N$ share the same continuous force.
If $g=p$, then $Y(t)=N(t)$ for every $t$ need not hold without $Y_0=N_0$ in comparable units.
The claim '$y$ grows because both $Y$ and $N$ grow' is not warranted without comparing $g$ and $p$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Constancy requires $g=p$; it is not automatic for arbitrary letters.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

$$g-p=0\iff g=p$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Same force letter means both aggregates use that common rate.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Equal forces preserve the ratio $Y/N$, but the levels themselves need not coincide.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Both growing is compatible with falling per capita when $p>g$. The comparison is essential.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Per capita freezes iff $g=p$. Equal forces do not equate levels. Growth of both aggregates does not imply growth of the ratio.

tasks.title: Semi-log decay graph — reading negative letter force
tasks.context: The figure illustrates $\ln P$ for a decaying continuous exponential $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with $k<0$. Claims use the letter $k$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The semi-log slope equals $|k|$ (unsigned) even when $k<0$.
Half-life does not equal $\dfrac{\ln 2}{k}$ when $k<0$, because that expression is negative.
On the semi-log plot, equal horizontal steps produce equal vertical drops.
Because the semi-log plot is linear, the raw $P$-plot is also linear.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$\frac{d}{dt}\ln P=k$$

Slope carries the signed force $k$, which is negative in decay.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Half-life must be positive; the correct formula uses $|k|$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$T_{1/2}=\frac{\ln 2}{|k|}$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Linearity of $\ln P$ means constant slope, hence equal run produces equal rise/drop.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Linearity after logs still leaves an exponential in the original level.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Negative semi-log slope is the force $k<0$. Half-life uses $|k|$. Equal steps on a line give equal log drops; raw levels stay curved.

tasks.title: Table that breaks pure exponential structure
tasks.context: A proposed table for a positive series is shown below in letters $P_0>0$ and $k\neq 0$. Decide whether a pure continuous exponential can generate it. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The successive ratios $P(1)/P(0)$ and $P(2)/P(1)$ are equal for every $k\neq 0$.
The successive ratios disagree only when $k=0$.
No choice of force makes this table a sampling of $P_0 e^{kt}$ at $t=0,1,2$.
Replacing the $t=2$ entry by $P_0 e^{2k}$ would restore pure continuous-exponential structure.
The displayed $t=2$ entry equals $P_0 e^{2k}$ for every $k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$\frac{P(1)}{P(0)}=e^{k}$$

$$\frac{P(2)}{P(1)}=\frac{e^{k}+e^{2k}}{e^{k}}=1+e^{k}$$

These are unequal for every real $k$, so the universal equality claim is false.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → False

The ratios $e^{k}$ and $1+e^{k}$ disagree for every real $k$, including $k\neq 0$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Pure continuous exponentials need constant ratios; this table lacks them.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The corrected triple $(P_0,P_0 e^{k},P_0 e^{2k})$ is exactly the exponential sample.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

$$P_0 e^{k}+P_0 e^{2k}=P_0 e^{2k}\iff e^{k}=0$$

which never holds, so the displayed entry is not $P_0 e^{2k}$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Compare successive ratios. The given $t=2$ entry spoils constancy, so the table is not pure exponential; correcting it to $P_0 e^{2k}$ restores the model.

tasks.title: Batch of continuous-exponential algebraic identities
tasks.context: Assume $P(t)=P_0 e^{kt}$ with $P_0>0$. Treat $k,t,s$ as real letters. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $P(t)+P(s)=P(t+s)$ fails for some $t,s$ (exponentials are not additive).
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$P(t+s)=P_0 e^{k(t+s)}=P(t)e^{ks}$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$P(t)P(s)=P_0^{2} e^{k(t+s)}=P_0\cdot P(t+s)$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$\frac{P(t)}{P(s)}=e^{k(t-s)}$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Exponentials satisfy multiplicative Cauchy laws, not additive ones. For $t=s=1$, $2P_0 e^{k}\neq P_0 e^{2k}$ whenever $e^{k}\neq 2$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

$$\bigl(P(t)/P_0\bigr)^{n}=e^{knt}=P(nt)/P_0$$

hence $P(nt)=P_0(P(t)/P_0)^{n}$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Continuous exponentials are multiplicative in time shifts. Products introduce an extra $P_0$; sums do not recombine into $P(t+s)$.

tasks.title: Parametric mix — capital, labour, and per-worker output
tasks.context: In a lettered Solow-style sketch, capital-like output $Y=Y_0 e^{gt}$ and labour $N=N_0 e^{pt}$ yield per-worker output $y=Y/N$. Forces $g,p$ are letters; no huge numeric GDP figures appear. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Per-worker force is not the product $gp$.
If $g>p$, per-worker output is strictly increasing.
If $g>0$, per-worker output is strictly increasing regardless of $p$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

$$y=y_0 e^{(g-p)t}$$

The force is the difference $g-p$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Log-ratios differentiate to a difference of forces, never a product $gp$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Force $g-p>0$ makes $y$ strictly increasing.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A large population force can dominate a positive $g$ and drive $y$ down.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

$$T=\frac{\ln 2}{g-p}$$

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Close with the difference force $g-p$: monotonicity and doubling time both read off $g-p$, never a product $gp$, and never $g$ alone.

tasks.title: Reading a base-two logarithm from its graph
tasks.context: The figure shows $f(x)=\log_{2}(x)$ for $x>0$. Use intercepts, the asymptote, and marked points. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graph meets the horizontal axis at $x=1$, so $f(1)=0$.
For every base $b>1$ the logarithm is strictly decreasing.
Zero arguments are always allowed in log domains.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

By definition $\log_{b}(1)=0$.

$$f(1)=\log_{2}1=0$$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Bases $b>1$ make $\log_{b}$ strictly increasing.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Base $2>1$ makes $f$ strictly increasing.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The argument of a logarithm must be strictly positive.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Half is $2^{-1}$, so

$$\log_{2}(1/2)=-1$$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Recover intercept $(1,0)$, asymptote $x=0$, increasing shape, and $\log_{2}(2^{k})=k$.

tasks.title: Change-of-base identity in a verification table
tasks.context: A student checks $\log_{b}a=\ln a/\ln b$ on lettered pairs $(P)$, $(Q)$, $(R)$ in the table. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Inverse partners $b^{t}$ and $\log_{b}$ share one common domain.
The identity fails whenever $a$ and $b$ are integers.
Pair $P$ yields a ratio strictly less than $2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$\log_{2}8=\frac{\ln 8}{\ln 2}=3$$

because $8=2^{3}$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$\log_{3}9=\frac{\ln 9}{\ln 3}=2$$

because $9=3^{2}$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Their domains are complementary: $\mathbb{R}$ versus $(0,\infty)$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The identity holds for all $a>0$ and $b>0$, $b
eq 1$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Pair $P$ gives $3>2$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Change-of-base once: $P\to 3$, $Q\to 2$, $R\to 2$.

tasks.title: Letter identities for product, quotient, and power laws
tasks.context: Let $a>0$, $b>0$, and $c\in\mathbb{R}$. Work with a fixed base $>1$ written $\log$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $\log(a^{c})=c\log a$ for all $a>0$ and all real $c$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Product law: $$\log(ab)=\log a+\log b$$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Quotient law: $$\log(a/b)=\log a-\log b$$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Counter-example: $\log(1+1)=\log 2
eq 0=\log 1+\log 1$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Power law: $$\log(a^{c})=c\log a$$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Left side $2\log a$; right side $(\log a)^{2}$ — not an identity.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Keep product/quotient/power; reject addition-inside and square confusions.
tasks.tables_markdown:
| Law | Letter form |
| --- | --- |
| Product | $\log(ab)=\log a+\log b$ |
| Quotient | $\log(a/b)=\log a-\log b$ |
| Power | $\log(a^{c})=c\log a$ |

tasks.title: Parametric domain of a product-argument logarithm
tasks.context: Fix $p<q$ and set $$f(x)=\log\bigl((x-p)(q-x)\bigr)$$ with base $>1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The natural domain of $f$ is the open interval $(p,q)$.
The endpoints $x=p$ and $x=q$ belong to the domain.
The product law $\log(uv)=\log u+\log v$ holds for $u,v>0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Need $(x-p)(q-x)>0$. With $p<q$ that holds on $(p,q)$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Endpoints make the argument $0$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Each midpoint factor equals $(q-p)/2>0$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Standard logarithm product law.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

On $(p,q)$ both factors are positive, so the product law applies.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Domain $(p,q)$; endpoints out; split logs only there.

tasks.title: Rebuild the base from intercept and unit point
tasks.context: A curve $f(x)=\log_{b}(x)$ with $b>1$ has asymptote $x=0$, intercept $(1,0)$, and $f(3)=1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The power law $\log(a^{c})=c\log a$ holds for $a>0$.
The same curve is the inverse of $g(t)=3^{t}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$\log_{b}b=1$ and $f(3)=1$ force $b=3$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$\log_{3}9=\log_{3}(3^{2})=2$$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Standard logarithm power law.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The inverse of $3^{t}$ is $\log_{3}$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

By definition the log of $1$ vanishes.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: From $f(3)=1$ rebuild $b=3$; use powers and the inverse relation.

tasks.title: Nested base-two logarithm: domain before evaluation
tasks.context: Consider $$h(x)=\log_{2}\bigl(\log_{2} x\bigr)$$ defined only where every intermediate argument is admissible. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Addition inside a logarithm is a universal law: $\log(a+b)=\log a+\log b$.
Zero arguments are always allowed in log domains.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Outer log needs $\log_{2}x>0$, i.e. $x>1$. Domain $(1,\infty)$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

No such identity holds on $a,b>0$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

The argument of a logarithm must be strictly positive.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

$$h(4)=\log_{2}2=1$$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

At $x=1$, $\log_{2}1=0$ and $\log_{2}0$ is undefined.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Need $\log_{2}x>0\Rightarrow x>1$; then evaluate at powers of two.

tasks.title: Inverse pair $2^{t}$ and $\log_{2}$ on matching domains
tasks.context: Let $g(t)=2^{t}$ for all real $t$ and $f(x)=\log_{2}x$ for $x>0$. The figure sketches both. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $f$ and $g$ have the same natural domain.
For every base $b>1$ the logarithm is strictly decreasing.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$\log_{2}(2^{t})=t$$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$2^{\log_{2}x}=x$$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

$g$ has domain $\mathbb{R}$; $f$ has domain $(0,\infty)$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Bases $b>1$ make $\log_{b}$ strictly increasing.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

$f(-1)$ is undefined.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Inverse identities hold on matching domains; the domains themselves differ.

tasks.title: Text-dense compound domain for a quotient argument
tasks.context: Let $$F(x)=\log\!\left(\frac{x-a}{b-x}\right)$$ with fixed $a<b$ and base $>1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The domain of $F$ is the closed interval $[a,b]$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

On $(a,b)$ both factors are positive.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Endpoints make the argument $0$ or undefined; domain is $(a,b)$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

At the midpoint the quotient equals $1$, and $\log 1=0$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

On $(a,b)$ the quotient law applies.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

At $x=b$ the denominator is zero.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Positive quotient on $(a,b)$; midpoint gives $\log 1=0$; exclude endpoints.

tasks.title: Tangled domain of a rational-argument logarithm
tasks.context: Consider $$m(x)=\log\!\left(\frac{2x+1}{x-3}\right)$$ with base $>1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $x=0$ is excluded because the argument is negative.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Sign chart about $-1/2$ and $3$ yields that union.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

At $x=3$ the quotient is undefined.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

At $x=0$ the quotient equals $-1/3<0$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

At $x=-1$ the quotient equals $1/2>0$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

On $(3,\infty)$ both factors are positive.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Critical points $-1/2$ and $3$; split logs safely on $(3,\infty)$.

tasks.title: Symbolic price elasticity from a log-log demand
tasks.context: Demand is $Q=A P^{-\beta}$ with $A>0$, $\beta>0$. Elasticity means $E=\dfrac{d\ln Q}{d\ln P}$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Taking logs yields $\ln Q=\ln A-\beta\ln P$.
The elasticity equals $-\beta$ at every price $P>0$.
Quotient law $\log(a/b)=\log a-\log b$ holds for $a,b>0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$\ln Q=\ln A-\beta\ln P$$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Differentiate w.r.t. $\ln P$: $$E=-\beta$$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Standard logarithm quotient law.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

If $\beta>1$ then $|E|=\beta>1$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

By definition the log of the base equals $1$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: From $\ln Q=\ln A-\beta\ln P$ read constant elasticity $E=-\beta$.

tasks.title: Comparing two logarithmic graphs that share an asymptote
tasks.context: The figure shows $f(x)=\log_{2}x$ and $g(x)=\log_{4}x$ on $(0,\infty)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Both graphs share the vertical asymptote $x=0$.
Zero arguments are always allowed in log domains.
Nested logarithms are defined for every $x>0$ without further checks.
Change-of-base works only with auxiliary base $10$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Every log with base $>1$ has asymptote $x=0$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The argument of a logarithm must be strictly positive.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Each outer log still needs a positive inner value.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

$$f(16)=4 eq 2=g(16)$$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Any valid auxiliary base $k>0$, $k

tasks.title: Text-dense: proving and disproving a claimed log identity chain
tasks.context: Claimed chain for $a,b>0$: $$\log a-\log b=\log\!\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)=\frac{\log a}{\log b}.$$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The first equality holds for all $a,b>0$.
The second equality holds for all $a,b>0$ with $b\neq 1$ in the log base sense — actually, as written with the same $\log$, it fails in general.
Counter-example: $a=e^{2}$, $b=e$ yields left side $1$ and right side $2$.
Change-of-base works only with auxiliary base $10$.
Replacing the second step by change-of-base $\log_{b}a=\ln a/\ln b$ repairs the chain.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Quotient law.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The jump to a quotient of logs is illegitimate.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$\log(e^{2}/e)=\log e=1$$ while $(\log e^{2})/(\log e)=2/1=2$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Any valid auxiliary base $k>0$, $k
eq 1$ works.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Change-of-base uses a different base in the subscript; it does not salvage the written chain with a single $\log$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Quotient law is fine; dividing logs is not; change-of-base is a different statement.
